prize_parts.citation: for establishing, through experiments on ruthenium-modified proteins, how electrons tunnel over long distances through protein matrices
for the development of base editing, programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: Gray and Winkler's long-range protein electron transfer is the only shortlisted line that rests on a clean physical mechanism, tested by time-resolved kinetics, with a compact two-person credit that fits the three-laureate limit and leaves Marcus theory (1992) as the settled theoretical backdrop. The distance-dependence and tunnelling-pathway picture is textbook and underlies respiration and photosynthesis, so recognition is mature, arguably late, and the priority question is easy to state. I pair it with base editing because the discussion shows B060 is the one candidacy ranked across the committee from several different fields (Aqvist, Chabes, Linke, Sparr, Somfai and Zou all place it), and Liu is the decisive originator, so a single-name credit uses only one slot and keeps the union at three. The two parts are distinct achievements, a fundamental physical-mechanistic result and a new chemical capability, which is a balanced prize.
statement.case_against: B030 was ranked by me alone in the openings and has no first-place or top-three support from anyone else, so I must not mistake my own field affinity for committee merit. Its real weakness is that the work is a mature body of results with no single dated breakthrough, and some colleagues will call it incremental after Marcus. Base editing is young: clinical outcomes are early, and it follows the 2020 CRISPR prize, so it may look like a downstream extension. If the committee wants a prize with clear, broadly demonstrated impact and clean attribution, B023 is the stronger and better supported choice and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Buchwald and Hartwig's Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling is a simple, general method used for 25 years, and Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work is a precursor with a real priority claim but not the general catalytic method.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and consequence, and a Buchwald plus Hartwig prize is the most defensible two-person attribution on the shortlist. My qualification is procedural: the 2010 cross-coupling prize already honoured the Pd-catalysis tradition, and the expert report must say what is new in chemical principle beyond ligand optimisation of that framework. As Secretary I would also want the Kosugi priority question settled in the written record rather than dismissed in discussion, since the Academy will be asked to justify omitting him. I keep it as my first alternative, not my lead.

responses.point: Nanopore sensing rests on a clear physical principle, ionic-current blockade, and delivered portable long-read sequencing; Kasianowicz, Deamer, Branton, Bayley and Akeson all contributed.
responses.response: I share your physicist's appreciation for the principle and for a method that made single molecules visible. My concern is attribution: the prize needs three names from at least five serious claimants (Kasianowicz, Branton, Deamer, Bayley, Akeson), and the decisive step, enzyme-controlled ratcheting for base reading, belongs to Akeson and Bayley's engineering while the 1996 translocation demonstration belongs to others. Unless the expert report separates concept, pore engineering and strand control cleanly, any trio will be contested, so I treat it as an alternative and not the lead.

responses.point: Condensate formation by phase separation is a new organising principle for the cell and is physical chemistry at its core, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the clearest founders.
responses.response: I take the physical-chemistry framing seriously and I value the conceptual shift. I disagree on timing and on evidence: whether specific in vivo condensates are genuinely phase-separated, and what function that separation serves, is still disputed, and that is a statement about the mechanism, which is where I want the field to be settled. Your own opening notes the debate. I also see the leaving-out of Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar work gives the quantitative physics, as a real attribution cost. I would revisit it when the in vivo evidence is firmer.

responses.point: Base editors fuse a deaminase to a Cas9 nickase to make defined C-to-T and A-to-G changes without double-strand breaks, with Liu as originator and Komor and Gaudelli as decisive trainees; propose Liu alone.
responses.response: I agree with Liu alone. It is the cleanest attribution, it follows the Committee's usual practice of crediting the principal investigator, and it leaves room for a second achievement. I take the Kondo and Nishida Target-AID question raised by Linke and Åqvist as an open point to be settled by the reports, not a reason to add names now. Where I differ is on the case against: the 2020 CRISPR prize and early clinical outcomes make this a young candidacy, so I would pair it with a mature mechanistic part rather than let it carry the prize alone.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports find B030 sufficiently distinct in chemical novelty from the Marcus-theory recognition of 1992 to justify a prize now.
Whether base editing is mature enough, given early clinical outcomes and the 2020 CRISPR prize, and whether Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID needs crediting.
Whether the committee prefers one strongly supported achievement (B023) to a two-part prize built from lower-ranked candidacies.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates. My research is on proton and electron transfer in respiratory enzymes, which is adjacent to B030; I have no personal or institutional tie to Gray or Winkler in my profile. My Stockholm University colleague Xiaodong Zou is a committee member, but none of her ranked candidates is in my configuration.
